title: Complexity of the Model Checking problem for inquisitive propositional and modal logic
text:
The aim of this paper is to study the complexity of the model checking problem {\mathsf{MC}} for inquisitive propositional logic \mathsf{InqB} and for inquisitive modal logic \mathsf{InqM}, that is, the problem of deciding whether a given finite structure for the logic satisfies a given formula. In particular, we prove that both problems are {\mathsf{AP}} -complete.

Inquisitive logics are a family of formalisms that extend classical and non-classical logic to encompass questions. Traditionally, logic is concerned with statements, that is, expressions completely determined by their truth-conditions. The standard approaches to semantics are based on this assumption and are usually formulated in terms of truth-assignment (e.g., Boolean valuations in propositional logic). However, this semantical approach does not allow us to study expressions whose meaning is not determined in terms of truth-conditions, such as questions.

In order to interpret questions, which are not true or false, the semantics of Inquisitive logic is based on a relation called support between and information states and a sentence. This allows to give a uniform semantic account for statement and questions alike: an information state supports a statement if it implies the statement; and it supports a question if it resolves the question.

The particular instances of inquisitive logic we consider in this paper are \mathsf{InqB} and \mathsf{InqM}, extending propositional logic and modal logic respectively with the question-forming operators. In these systems information states are formalized as sets of truth-assignments, which gives us a much richer semantical structure than in the classical setting. The main question we tackle in this paper is: how hard is it to decide if a formula of \mathsf{InqB} (resp., \mathsf{InqM}) is supported by an information state in a given model ?

The problem of deciding whether a formula \phi of a logic L is satisfied by a model \mathcal{M} is referred to as the model checking problem for L (in symbols {\mathsf{MC}}(L)). The computational complexity of this problem is known for several logics (see, e.g., [2] for an overview of the classical results). In recent years, the problem has been addressed also for a class of logics called team logics which, like our inquisitive systems, are interpreted relative to sets of assignments (see, e.g., [3,4] and [5]).

Although there is a close connection between these logics and inquisitive logics, it was still an open question what are the complexities of {\mathsf{MC}}(\mathsf{InqB}) and {\mathsf{MC}}(\mathsf{InqM}). In this paper we give a reduction of the {\mathsf{PSPACE}} -complete problem true quantified Boolean formulas {\mathsf{TQBF}} (see, e.g., [7]) to {\mathsf{MC}}(\mathsf{InqB}), thus settling that both {\mathsf{MC}}(\mathsf{InqB}) and {\mathsf{MC}}(\mathsf{InqM}) are {\mathsf{PSPACE}} -complete.

The paper is structured as follows: In Section 2 we present the basic notions of inquisitive logic used throughout the paper. In Section 3 we introduce suitable encodings of \mathsf{InqB} and \mathsf{InqM} structures and formalize the model checking problems {\mathsf{MC}}(\mathsf{InqB}) and {\mathsf{MC}}(\mathsf{InqM}). Moreover, in the same section we present an algorithm for alternating Turing machines to solve {\mathsf{MC}}(\mathsf{InqM}) and use it to show that {\mathsf{MC}}(\mathsf{InqM}) —and a fortiori also {\mathsf{MC}}(\mathsf{InqBQ}) —is in the class {\mathsf{PSPACE}}. In Section 4 we present and study a polynomial-space reduction of the {\mathsf{TQBF}} problem to the {\mathsf{MC}}(\mathsf{InqB}), thus showing that the problem is also {\mathsf{PSPACE}} -hard, and we thus infer that {\mathsf{MC}}(\mathsf{InqB}) and {\mathsf{MC}}(\mathsf{InqM}) are both {\mathsf{PSPACE}} -complete. We conclude in Section 5 with some remarks and directions for future work.
